passage:
Friday, 11 p.m.
The entrance results came at four. I didn't make the list. Not even the waiting list.
I keep thinking: I'm just stupid. All those coaching fees Papa paid, all of Mummy's early mornings packing my tiffin, and I've wasted it. I'm a burden, that's the truth. Rahul uncle's son got in on his first try, and everyone will ask on Sunday.
I didn't come out for dinner. Around ten Gautam bhaiya knocked and didn't leave when I said go away. He sat on the floor, and I told him what I'd been writing, the burden part too. He went quiet, then said, "Hansa, one test is not you," and went straight to get Mummy. She sat on my bed, held my hand and said nobody in this house thinks that, not for one second. She's sleeping in my room tonight. Tomorrow she wants us to see the school counsellor together.
I still feel stupid. But less alone.

qa.q: When did the entrance results come?
qa.a: The entrance results came at four.

qa.q: What does Hansa's word "burden" reveal about how Hansa feels?
qa.a: Hansa feels deeply ashamed and worthless, turning one failed test into a verdict on the whole self and the family's sacrifices.

qa.q: What made that night's response a good one?
qa.a: Gautam stayed despite being told to go and fetched Mummy at once; she reassured Hansa, stayed close all night and planned a visit to the counsellor.

qa.q: What might Gautam have felt hearing the burden part?
qa.a: He likely felt alarmed and deeply worried, which is why he went quiet and brought Mummy right away.

grounding: Shows a teen turning a failed entrance test into a verdict of being stupid and a burden, and family responding the same night.

passage: "Minakshi, since you won't show your mother the report card, let your Rekha bua tell you what I did at fifteen. I failed the half-yearly maths paper. Twenty-eight out of a hundred. And do you know what I told everyone? The paper was out of syllabus. The teacher hated me. My pen leaked. The fan was too noisy. Each story was a little bit true, and together they made one big lie. I hid the report card inside my geography book for three weeks and told Amma the results weren't out yet. By the finals I had the same gaps, because I had never looked at a single wrong answer. Then my cousin found the card and, instead of shouting, sat with me and went through the paper question by question. That was the first time I learned anything from it."

qa.q: What did young Rekha score in the half-yearly maths paper?
qa.a: Twenty-eight out of a hundred.

qa.q: Why did young Rekha keep blaming the paper, the teacher and the fan?
qa.a: She was ashamed and scared, and blaming others shielded her from the pain of failing.

qa.q: What choice inside the story finally helped?
qa.a: Going through the paper question by question with the cousin, instead of hiding the card, let her learn from what went wrong.

qa.q: What might the cousin have felt on finding the hidden card?
qa.a: The cousin may have been surprised but chose kindness over shouting, wanting to help rather than punish.

grounding: Shows a teen blaming the paper, the teacher and luck and hiding the result from family, which shields from pain but blocks learning.

passage: "Harsha, you asked how I became the cousin everyone calls when results come out. It started one Diwali, when I was twenty and my cousin Keshav was sixteen. His board results had come out badly that week. At the family lunch, Mausi, Mama, everybody went round the table: 'Sharma ji's son got ninety-five.' 'Your sister topped at your age.' Keshav kept his eyes on his plate and didn't eat. I felt sick watching it. After lunch I found him alone on the roof. I didn't give advice. I said, 'One result is not you, Keshav. I know you.' Then: 'Want to sit down next week and plan what's next? Only if you want.' He nodded. We made a plan with his teacher. Your Madhav chacha has kept that habit ever since."

qa.q: What did a relative say about Sharma ji's son?
qa.a: That Sharma ji's son got ninety-five.

qa.q: What did young Madhav feel watching the lunch-table comparisons?
qa.a: He felt sick and upset, watching Keshav stare at his plate while the relatives compared.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made a difference for Keshav?
qa.a: Madhav found him alone, said one result was not him and offered to plan next steps together, which led to a plan with his teacher.

qa.q: What was the lunch like for Keshav?
qa.a: Keshav felt humiliated and small, keeping his eyes on his plate and unable to eat.

grounding: Shows a cousin watching a teen compared with others after a bad result, then offering a quiet word and help planning next steps.

passage: The hostel common room was loud with a cricket match on TV, but Kunal sat by the window holding the letter from the pilot selection board. Not recommended. Since he was nine he had pictured himself in a flight suit; he had even practised the salute in the mirror. Now that future had simply closed. On his phone, a batchmate was posting photos from the academy gates, grinning, and Kunal felt a sharp stab of envy, then guilt for feeling it. Irfan dropped onto the sofa beside him. "Bro, forget it. You'll crack something better. It's a sign." Kunal nodded and said nothing. Later, alone on the terrace, he let himself cry for the nine-year-old in the flight suit. He didn't know yet what came next. For tonight, not knowing was allowed.

qa.q: What did the letter from the pilot selection board say?
qa.a: Not recommended.

qa.q: What did Kunal feel seeing the batchmate's photos?
qa.a: A sharp stab of envy, then guilt for feeling it.

qa.q: Why is Kunal's crying on the terrace a healthy step?
qa.a: Letting himself grieve the lost future, instead of rushing to Irfan's positive story, is part of moving on.

qa.q: How does Irfan seem to see Kunal's loss?
qa.a: Irfan means well and wants to cheer Kunal up quickly, not seeing that Kunal first needs to grieve.

grounding: Shows a young adult mourning a long-pictured future with sadness, envy and doubt, and allowing the grief instead of rushing to a positive story.

passage: Three months after we shut the café in Bandra, Aparna and I finally sat down with a notebook and the old accounts. In the first weeks after closing, I had swung between two stories: it was all my fault, or it was all the landlord's and the road works' fault. Neither was fair. So we drew three columns. What we controlled: we opened too big, we changed the menu five times, I hired friends I couldn't manage. What was luck: the road dug up for eight months, the rent going up. What to change next time: start smaller, test one menu for a season, hire for skills. Aparna tapped the page and said, "Zubin, look. It's not a verdict. It's a list." It was strangely calming. For the first time, the café felt less like a wound and more like information.

qa.q: What were the three columns?
qa.a: What we controlled, what was luck, and what to change next time.

qa.q: How did the three-column review make Zubin feel?
qa.a: Zubin felt strangely calm, as the café turned from a wound into information.

qa.q: Why was the review better than the two stories Zubin had swung between?
qa.a: It gave a fair look at causes, neither total self-blame nor total excuses, so the failure produced lessons to act on.

qa.q: How does Aparna seem to see the failure?
qa.a: Aparna sees it as a list to learn from, not a verdict on either of them.

grounding: Shows a fair review after a failed venture, sorting what was in their control, what was luck and what to change, turning failure into information.

passage:
August. Nitin had not opened his design software since losing the agency client in June. When Arnab asked him for a simple poster for the bakery's Onam sale, he almost said no. He made it in one evening. By the weekend, three customers had asked Arnab who designed it.
September. A neighbour asked Nitin for a small logo for her tuition classes. He sent three options, two days early, and she chose the second one without changes. He printed it and stuck it above his desk.
October. Nitin walked into an interview for a junior designer role, the poster and the logo in his portfolio. Halfway through answering a question about deadlines, he noticed something: his voice wasn't shaking. He had not thought his way back to confidence. He had made his way back, one small job at a time.

qa.q: What did Arnab ask Nitin to design in August?
qa.a: A simple poster for the bakery's Onam sale.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel by the time of the October interview?
qa.a: He felt steadier and more confident, noticing that his voice wasn't shaking.

qa.q: Why did starting with a small poster help Nitin?
qa.a: Small, doable jobs gave him real wins, so confidence came back through action rather than thinking.

qa.q: What might Arnab have hoped when asking for the poster?
qa.a: Arnab may have wanted to ease Nitin back into design gently, with a low-pressure job between friends.

grounding: Shows a person trying again at a smaller scale after a setback, collecting small wins until confidence returns through action.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage: On my first day at the logistics software company, I wore the new shirt Amma had ironed twice. The office had bean bags and a coffee machine I didn't know how to use. By ten I was in a stand-up meeting where people said "sprint velocity", "blockers" and "push to staging" as if everyone was born knowing them. I nodded. I wrote the words in my notebook to search later. Abhinav, my buddy for the week, asked, "Yogesh, anything blocking you?" I said, "No, all good," though I couldn't even log into the laptop. At lunch I kept thinking, maybe HR mixed up two CVs. Maybe the real Yogesh is sitting at home. Then I'd remember the offer email, and a small, fizzy excitement would come back. I went home both terrified and thrilled.

qa.q: What did Yogesh write in the notebook?
qa.a: The unfamiliar words, to search later.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Yogesh go home with?
qa.a: Yogesh went home both terrified and thrilled, worried the selection was a mistake yet excited about the job.

qa.q: What small step could help Yogesh on day two?
qa.a: Telling Abhinav honestly about the laptop login and asking what one or two of the terms mean.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see Yogesh on day one?
qa.a: Abhinav likely sees a new joiner who says all is good, not knowing Yogesh could not even log in.

grounding: Shows a fresh graduate on day one surrounded by confident colleagues and unfamiliar terms, excited to be hired but worried it was a mistake.

passage:
"Pranav? It's ten. Why are you still here?" Rekha stopped by his desk, bag on her shoulder.
"Just finishing something." He minimised a tutorial video.
"What something? The API task? I gave you that as a two-day thing."
"Yeah. I'm almost there. I wanted to read up on how the login part works first."
"You could have asked me. It's a fifteen-minute explanation."
"I didn't want to bother you. Everyone's so busy." He rubbed his eyes. "And it's basic. I should know it."
"Who told you that?"
"Nobody. I'm the only one here from a small college. I don't want anyone to think they made a mistake."
Rekha put her bag down. "So you've been here till ten every night for two weeks, learning things I could show you in minutes."
Pranav said nothing.
"Tomorrow, eleven o'clock. Bring your questions. All of them."

qa.q: What time was it when Rekha found Pranav at his desk?
qa.a: It was ten at night.

qa.q: Why hasn't Pranav asked Rekha for help?
qa.a: He feels anxious and insecure, afraid that asking basic questions will show he doesn't belong.

qa.q: What does Rekha's offer change for Pranav?
qa.a: A set time to bring all his questions makes asking normal, so he can learn in minutes instead of hiding gaps till ten each night.

qa.q: What might Rekha realise when Pranav explains?
qa.a: Rekha seems to realise he has struggled alone for two weeks out of fear, and she moves to make asking easy.

grounding: Shows a new hire staying late and studying in secret rather than asking questions, which feels safer but slows learning.
